newsitem.title: USA: CSCE coffee ends higher in sluggish trading.
newsitem.headline: CSCE coffee ends higher in sluggish trading.

text.p: CSCE coffee futures settled mostly higher in light dealings Monday, lifted by local and light speculative buying as dwindling exchange-certified coffee stocks kept the market underpinned, traders said.

Benchmark July arabicas closed up 3.15 cents at 196.40 cents a lb after posting trades between 197.50 and 192.00 cents. Spot May finished up 3.90 at 220.25, while the outer months ended 4.75 higher to 3.40 lower.
The nearby May/July switch, a barometer of nearby availability, widened to 23.85 today from 23.10 at the close on Friday.

Coffee prices came in mixed at the outset -- failing to reach their 2.00-3.00 cents higher opening due -- after a round of trade selling offset early buy orders, dealers said. But the market managed to bounce back and spent the bulk of the day in positive territory, supported by ongoing supply concerns, traders said.
Traders said the steady decline of CSCE certified coffee stocks from a buildup of more than 83,000 60-kg bags three weeks ago has helped fuel supply jitters.
The exchange reported after Friday's close that certified coffee stocks fell 1,747 60-kg bags, to 48,603 bags -- or about 195 lots -- as of April 24.
Meanwhile, open interest on the May contract, which expires in three weeks, stood at 2,626 lots as of Friday's close.
"There are too many open positions in May," said Refco analyst Ann Prendergast. "The likelyhood is that there is going to be some squeeze between now and mid-May."
"I expect there will be extreme volatility and rising prices from delivery fears," she added.
After Monday's close, the CSCE reported certified coffee stocks were unchanged, at 48,603 bags as of April 25. There were 3,815 bags of coffee pending grading, the exchange said.
Traders said the market's focus was likely to turn towards top-grower Brazil as it approaches winter and the harvest of the 1997/98 crop begins.
A forecaster at Brazil's National Institute of Meteorology (Inmet) said the country's winter should not be as cold as last year's, but he did not rule out the possibility of frosts in coffee areas.
"This should not be a harsh winter this year, temperatures should be more or less normal but there is still the risk of frosts in the coffee areas," said Francisco Assis.
The greatest risk of frost would be from the second half of June and run through to the end of July, he said.

Technically, traders said July would face strong psychological resistance at the 200.00 level. The next upside hurdle was seen at 203.50 cents, a life-of-contract high set on Friday. Support at today's low of 192.00 cents.
The day's volume was light, at an estimated 5,895 lots.
